fetched_contents.text: Language Learning in the Wild: The L2 Acquisition of English Restrictive Relative Clauses 1. Introduction Relative clause constructions have attracted sustained scholarly interest for over half a century (Roland et al., 2007), addressing a broad range of questions in first language acquisition (e.g., Diessel & Tomasello, 2000, 2005); second and third language acquisition (e.g., Flynn et al., 2004); adult sentence processing (e.g., Gibson, 1998); language typology (e.g., Keenan & Comrie, 1977); as well as grammatical theory (e.g., Alexiadou et al., 2000).1 Much research and theorizing addressing the acquisition of those constructions is articulated from a cognitive perspective (Doughty & Long, 2003), buttressed by an experimental infrastructure involving grammaticality judgements, sentence combinations tasks, elicitation and act out tasks, among a host of other techniques. In contrast with experimental research on relativization, the bulk of which has targeted perceptual issues relating to processing and decoding strategies (Romaine, 1984; Macdonald, 2015), corpus-based investigations of relative clauses in natural speech production data are much less common (but see e.g., Diessel & Tomasello, 2000; Ghafar Samar, 2000; Yip & Matthews, 2007). The fact that relative clauses are rare in running discourse (Milroy & Gordon, 2003) may explain the predilection for data elicited and analyzed in experimental conditions, although the extent to which findings generated in tightly controlled laboratory settings accurately reflect what transpires in real-world contexts remains a moot point (Jaeger, 2010; Speed et al., 2018). These concerns are symptomatic of the very issues that inspired the current research, in keeping with our goal of contributing to socially sensitive and ecologically valid models of L2 acquisition. We argue that the sociolinguistic investigation of everyday speech is a necessary complement to experimental research on L2 acquisition, as it can refine and subtly enhance our understanding of how relative clauses are acquired, precisely because such an approach engages with, rather than abstracts away from, the inherent variability endemic to natural speech situated in its social context (Labov, 1972a). Because this variability provides critical insights into the nature, extent, and limits of the L2 acquisition process, its correct characterization is of paramount importance in constructing theories of L2 acquisition that are accountable to actual usage facts. Major incentives for corpus-based studies of relativization have come from constructivist and usage-based investigations of language acquisition (see e.g., Diessel & Tomasello, 2000, 2005; Fox & Thompson, 2007; Wiechmann, 2015). These studies have catalyzed interest in arriving at a better understanding of the relative clause constructions that language learners encounter and acquire as a result of exposure to spontaneous speech. If, as usage-based theories posit, grammatical knowledge is predicated on speakers’ linguistic experience (Bybee, 2010), then it follows that the community-based speech varieties of the TL to which L2 speakers are exposed have the potential to afford insights into the structural biases in the TL input that intimately shape the acquisition process. Both naturalistic and experimental research on L1 acquisition has been instrumental in highlighting the effect of input frequencies on the development of relative clause constructions in child language (Lieven, 2010). As we show below, relative clause constructions in L2 acquisition are impacted by TL input frequency patterns too (see also Mellow, 2006). Among the key motivations for applying corpus-based approaches to informal social settings is the need to extend the purview of L2 research beyond formal language-learning environments to less formal ones (Bayley & Tarone, 2012), including naturalistic contexts, where the amount, frequency and type of input which learners encounter is said to be far less restricted than in classroom settings (Montrul, 2020). Sankoff et al. (1997, p. 193) argue that if L2 acquisition is more than the product of successful classroom-based learning, then it should exhibit properties of the TL vernacular which are not ordinarily transmitted to learners in academic settings, but are internalized by L2 speakers who have a high degree of contact with the TL community. The quantitative approach employed in the present study is ideally suited to elucidating vernacular patterns in L2 speech and ascertaining whether they are the product of vernacular transmission from the TL, the result of processes that are unique to L2 speech (i.e., interlanguage grammar; see Meyerhoff & Schleef, 2012), or the outcome of transfer effects from L2 speakers’ native language. Of the different kinds of relative clause that have attracted scholarly attention, the ones we privilege here are restrictive relative clauses. fetched_contents.text: Anticipating Explanations in Relative Clause Processing . Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2012 Jul 7. Abstract We show that comprehenders’ expectations about upcoming discourse coherence relations influence the resolution of local structural ambiguity. We employ cases in which two clauses share both a syntactic relationship and a discourse relationship, and hence in which syntactic and discourse processing might be expected to interact. An off-line sentence-completion study and an on-line self-paced reading study examined readers’ expectations for high/low relative clause attachments following implicit-causality and non-implicit-causality verbs (John detests/babysits the children of the musician who…). In the off-line study, the widely reported low-attachment preference for English is observed in the non-implicit causality condition, but this preference gives way to more high attachments in the implicit causality condition in cases in which (i) the verb’s causally implicated referent occupies the high-attachment position and (ii) the relative clause provides an explanation for the event described by the matrix clause (e.g., …who are arrogant and rude). In the on-line study, a similar preference for high attachment emerges in the implicit causality context—crucially, before the occurrence of any linguistic evidence that the RC does in fact provide an explanation—whereas the low-attachment preference is consistent elsewhere. These findings constitute the first demonstration that expectations about ensuing discourse coherence relationships can elicit full reversals in syntactic attachment preferences, and that these discourse-level expectations can affect on-line disambiguation as rapidly as lexical and morphosyntactic cues. Keywords: Discourse Processing, Relative Clause Attachment Ambiguity, Implicit Causality, Coherence Relations 1. Introduction As cognitive agents attempting to comprehend their world, people do not merely gather information through their senses about the situations they encounter. They also draw inferences necessary to interpret these situations as coherent. For example, if one encountered a scene in which an individual is lying dead on the floor and another is standing nearby with a gun, one would likely infer that the death was caused by the second individual having shot the first, despite not having witnessed the event firsthand. One might not reach the same conclusion if the individual standing nearby was instead holding a stethoscope, suggesting other possible causal connections, e.g., that a doctor is trying to help the person on the floor. Interpreting natural language discourses that describe such situations triggers the same type of inferential processes. For instance, upon hearing (1): (1) John detests his coworkers. They are arrogant and rude. a comprehender will typically not be content to merely interpret the two sentences as independent statements about the world, but will instead infer that the coworkers’ arrogance and rudeness are the reasons why John detests them. This inference comes naturally despite the fact that no linguistic material in the passage explicitly cues a causal relationship. Our comprehender might be confused, on the other hand, by the similarly unremarkable sentences in passage (2): (2) John detests his coworkers. They like curry. People typically detest other people for a reason, and hence this passage might lead our comprehender to wonder why liking curry would cause someone to detest someone else. The lack of an obvious causal connection might even lead the comprehender to construct a possible scenario by which the passage would become coherent: perhaps John doesn’t like the smell of curry, and his coworkers regularly have it for lunch in cubicles proximal to his, for example. As pointed out by Hobbs (1979), the very fact that comprehenders are driven to entertain such scenarios demonstrates that they actively seek to establish the coherence of discourses. Despite the fact that no linguistic element in (2) signals a causal relationship, it nonetheless seems that comprehenders have an expectation that such a relation exists—particularly so, as we will subsequently argue, with so-called implicit causality (IC) verbs like detest—and will consider making additional assumptions about the state of the world to support the inference of this relation. Such facts have led a number of researchers (Hobbs, 1979; Kehler, 2002; Asher and Lascarides, 2003, inter alia) to argue that the establishment of such relevancy relations—henceforth, coherence relations, of which the causal Explanation relation in (1) is one example—is a fundamental and ubiquitous aspect of discourse interpretation. That is, just as comprehenders seek to recover the implicit syntactic structure of a sequence of words in a sentence, they likewise attempt to recover the implicit “coherence structure” of a sequence of utterances in a discourse. If comprehenders establish such coherence relations and, as has been posited to occur for syntactic relations, generate expectations about what relations are likely to ensue based on the current context, one can ask whether the impact of such expectations extends beyond discourse to the level of syntactic structure building. Mini-report on the main elicitation methods used in relative clause studies

The literature most commonly uses a small set of elicitation formats, with sentence repetition/imitation, picture description, and fill-in-the-blank/sentence-completion tasks being especially prominent. A review of relative clause production methods notes that a more controlled production task type is elicited imitation (or sentence repetition), in which participants are asked to repeat what they hear or read [N6-R2]. Picture description is also widely used because it provides concrete context and can be adapted to test multiple relative clause types, such as subject and object clauses, with picture stimuli that depict reversible events [N2-R4]. Fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion formats are likewise common, as they are used in tests and comprehension tasks with blanks and multiple-choice options, and in materials modeled on relative clause production tasks [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. The same search results also point to elicited production as a core method in comparative studies of naturalistic corpora and elicited production experiments [N6-R5].

How each method structures the target clause and surrounding context varies accordingly. In sentence repetition/imitation, the target clause is embedded in a sentence or phrase that participants are asked to repeat, so the context is controlled and highly structured [N6-R2]. In picture description, the context is provided by visual stimuli, and the target clause is often inferred from the pictures rather than being directly stated [N2-R4]. In fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks, the context is usually a partially completed sentence, so the target clause is embedded in a grammatically incomplete structure that participants complete [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. The evidence also suggests that some studies use sentence-repetition tasks to measure the construct underlying an effect such as the NPAH effect, and that these tasks can be adapted to different relative clause types [N6-R2][N6-R4].

What kinds of responses are collected and how they are coded also differ by method. In sentence repetition/imitation, the response is a produced sentence or phrase, and coding typically involves checking whether the produced relative clause is present, correct, or not present, and whether it reflects the intended structure [N6-R2]. In picture-description tasks, responses are spoken or written descriptions that must be coded for the presence and type of relative clauses, and the coding may also assess whether the description is grammatically correct or appropriate given the picture [N2-R4]. In fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks, responses are usually multiple-choice or open-ended completions, and coding is based on whether the completed relative clause matches the target structure, especially for subject versus object relative clauses [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. The evidence also mentions spontaneous speech data, which are collected in naturalistic settings and are contrasted with elicited production data in experimental studies [N6-R3]. That contrast is relevant to coding because naturalistic data may require more lenient or context-sensitive coding than tightly controlled elicited responses [N6-R3].

Overall, the main elicitation formats are sentence repetition/imitation, picture description, fill-in-the-blank/sentence-completion tasks, and naturalistic elicited production. These formats structure the target clause within a controlled or contextualized prompt, and they collect responses that are then coded for relative clause presence, type, and correctness [N6-R2][N2-R4][N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-R4][N6-R3].

Mini-report on task design and participant burden

Task complexity can strongly influence elicited output quality. The evidence suggests that more complex or open-ended tasks may reduce the likelihood of mechanical responses, but also increase the risk of noise or inconsistent output. For example, picture-description tasks are described as being productive in some cases, but they also depend on participants’ ability to generate appropriate descriptions rather than simply selecting a pre-specified answer [N2-R3]. The same source notes that relative clause response types were examined in a table of responses, implying that output quality can vary depending on how clearly participants can produce the target structure [N2-R3]. The task-complexity literature also indicates that complexity can be reduced in operational execution and site burden domains, which is relevant to the idea that more complex elicitation formats may impose greater demands on participants [N5-R1]. This is consistent with the broader claim that task design features and participant characteristics affect study outcomes, including participant burden and data quality [N5-R4].

Participant burden changes across elicitation formats in predictable ways. Elicited production tasks, especially sentence repetition and picture description, are likely to be more burdensome than simple multiple-choice tasks because they require participants to generate speech or longer descriptions. By contrast, fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion formats are often less burdensome because they are shorter and more structured [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N6-R2]. The search results also point to adaptive elicitation and dynamic participant-responsive designs as ways to reduce cognitive fatigue and improve data accuracy, suggesting that burden-sensitive formats can mitigate the negative effects of task complexity [N5-R5]. This is especially important in relative clause studies, where participants may have to generate multiple responses or describe a scene, both of which can increase mental effort [N2-R4][N6-R2].

Task instructions and feedback also affect performance. In the provided evidence, picture-description tasks are used with stimuli that depict reversible events and are associated with multiple relative clause types, indicating that clear instructions are needed to guide participants toward the intended structure [N2-R4]. The literature on preference elicitation and choice tasks also emphasizes that cognitive burden varies with task design, and that feedback can reduce burden and improve accuracy [N5-R3]. While the evidence here is not directly about relative clause studies, it supports the general principle that explicit instructions and responsive feedback can reduce confusion and improve response quality [N5-R3][N5-R5]. The same point is reinforced by the emphasis on participant burden as a hidden constraint in clinical trials, which implies that even small changes in instructions or feedback can have meaningful effects on data collection [N5-R2].

In summary, task complexity can improve output quality when it encourages productive generation, but it can also introduce noise or inconsistency if participants struggle with the task. Participant burden is generally lower in simple, structured formats like fill-in-the-blank tasks and higher in open-ended formats like picture description or sentence repetition. Instructions and feedback matter because they can reduce burden and improve performance, especially when tasks are complex or adaptive [N2-R3][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5].

Mini-report on advantages and limitations of each method

Each method has a distinct usefulness and set of limitations. Sentence repetition/imitation is useful because it is highly controlled and directly measures the target construct, making it suitable for comparing different relative clause types or effects like the NPAH effect [N6-R2][N6-R3]. It is also convenient for collecting speech samples that can be coded for relative clause presence and structure [N6-R2]. Its main limitation is that it may produce highly artificial or rehearsed responses, especially if participants are over-trained or if the task is too narrow [N6-R3]. This can reduce ecological validity and make the data less representative of natural speech [N6-R3]. Implementation choices such as sentence length, repetition frequency, and whether feedback is provided can affect data quality, with more frequent repetition potentially improving accuracy at the cost of burden [N6-R2].

Picture-description tasks are useful because they provide concrete context and can be adapted to test multiple relative clause types, including subject and object clauses, with stimuli that depict reversible events [N2-R4]. They are also good for eliciting spontaneous-like output, as participants are asked to describe a scene rather than simply select an answer [N2-R4]. The limitation is that participants may vary widely in how much descriptive detail they provide, which can make coding less reliable and more context-dependent [N2-R4]. The same evidence also shows that these tasks can be productive in some cases, but not in others, suggesting that output quality is sensitive to participants’ language proficiency and task instructions [N2-R3]. Implementation choices such as stimulus selection, response length, and whether participants are asked to repeat or describe matter for data quality [N2-R4].

Fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks are useful because they are relatively simple, structured, and easy to score, especially when participants choose among options or complete a sentence [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. They are especially suitable for testing relative clause type differences and for controlling the context in which the target clause appears [N2-R1][N4-R4]. However, they are limited in ecological validity because they may encourage guessing, word-order recall, or grammatical guessing rather than genuine production [N2-R1][N4-R4]. Implementation choices such as the number of options, the presence of distractors, and the degree of open-endedness can affect both ease of scoring and the authenticity of the responses [N2-R1][N2-R2].

Naturalistic elicited production is useful when the goal is to approximate spontaneous speech and capture variability in relative clause use across contexts [N6-R3][N6-R5]. It is also valuable for comparing with corpus data and for studying how learners produce relative clauses in real-world settings [N6-R3][N6-R5]. Its main limitation is that spontaneous speech is difficult to standardize and may include irrelevant or digressive material that complicates coding [N6-R3]. It can also be subject to observer bias if researchers rely on retrospective or partial sampling rather than systematic collection [N6-R3]. Implementation choices such as sampling strategy, recording protocol, and corpus comparison can affect whether the data are representative and analyzable [N6-R3][N6-R5].

The evidence also points to broader methodological tradeoffs. Corpus-based studies are useful for capturing large-scale usage patterns and for investigating input frequency effects, but they are limited by the rarity of relative clauses in running discourse and by the difficulty of isolating the construct of interest [N3-F2]. Experimental studies are useful for controlling variables and measuring specific constructs, but they can lose ecological validity if the task is too artificial [N3-F2]. Adaptive elicitation and dynamic response sampling are useful for reducing cognitive fatigue and improving data accuracy, but they require careful design to avoid introducing new sources of bias [N5-R5]. Overall, the most useful methods depend on the research question: controlled imitation is best for direct elicitation and comparison, picture description is best for context-rich production, and naturalistic elicited production is best for ecological validity [N6-R2][N2-R4][N6-R3][N6-R5].

In sentence repetition/imitation, coding typically involves checking whether the produced relative clause is present, correct, or not present, and whether it reflects the intended structure [N6-R2]. In picture-description tasks, responses are coded for the presence and type of relative clauses, as well as for grammatical correctness or appropriateness to the stimulus [N2-R4]. In fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks, scoring is often based on whether the completed relative clause matches the target structure, especially for subject versus object relative clauses [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. The evidence also mentions corpus-based analysis and experimental elicitation, which suggests that coding can be more complex when combining naturalistic and experimental data [N3-F2].

Sources of intercoder reliability and annotation bias are well established in the evidence. Intercoder reliability is defined as the degree to which two analysts or coders agree on their decisions, such as which passages were coded in a particular way [N7-R3]. A separate source states that high intercoder reliability is required in qualitative content analysis when more than one coder is involved, and that ICR scores can be used as a heuristic tool in explorative studies to objectify or specify coding decisions [N7-R1][N7-R4]. This implies that coding relative clauses is especially sensitive to bias if coders differ in how they interpret context, grammatical correctness, or relative clause type. The evidence also suggests that coding and scoring are more challenging when responses are open-ended or when the target structure is ambiguous, because those cases require more judgment [N6-R2][N2-R4].

How corpus and experimental data differ in analysis is a key distinction. Corpus-based studies are useful for capturing large-scale usage patterns and for investigating input frequency effects, but they are limited by the rarity of relative clauses in running discourse and by the difficulty of isolating the construct of interest [N3-F2]. Experimental elicitation is useful for controlling variables and measuring specific constructs, but it can lose ecological validity if the task is too artificial [N3-F2]. The same source contrasts naturalistic or spontaneous speech data with elicited production data, noting that naturalistic data have limitations because the mere emergence of relative clauses may not reflect the underlying construct [N6-R3]. This matters for analysis because corpus data often require frequency-based or distributional analysis, while experimental data may be more suited to item analysis, response coding, or comparison of specific types [N3-F2][N6-R3].

Overall, coding, scoring, and analysis face challenges from ambiguity in responses, variation in coding decisions, and differences between corpus and experimental data. Intercoder reliability is a central concern, and annotation bias can arise when coders disagree on grammaticality, clause type, or context-appropriateness [N7-R3][N7-R1][N7-R4]. Corpus and experimental data differ in analysis because corpus data emphasize usage patterns and frequency, while experimental data emphasize controlled measurement and construct isolation [N3-F2][N6-R3].

## Integrated final answer on methods for eliciting relative clause production data

The literature on relative clause production data relies on a small set of commonly used elicitation methods, each of which structures the target clause differently and produces different kinds of responses that are then coded in distinct ways. The main formats identified in the branch reports are **sentence repetition/imitation**, **picture description**, **fill-in-the-blank/sentence-completion tasks**, and **naturalistic elicited production** [N6-R2][N2-R4][N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-R5]. These methods are chosen for different research purposes, and each has its own advantages and limitations that affect data quality, ecological validity, and analysis.

---

## 1) Main elicitation methods and how they structure the target clause

### Sentence repetition/imitation
This is one of the most commonly used controlled methods in relative clause studies. Participants are asked to repeat what they hear or read, making it a direct and highly structured way to elicit production [N6-R2]. The target clause is embedded in a sentence or phrase that participants must reproduce, so the context is tightly controlled [N6-R2]. This method is especially useful for comparing different relative clause types or for measuring the construct underlying an effect such as the NPAH effect [N6-R3].

### Picture description
In picture-description tasks, the context is provided by visual stimuli, and participants describe the scene or event depicted in the picture [N2-R4]. The target clause is often inferred from the picture, rather than being directly stated. Because the stimuli can depict reversible events, these tasks can be adapted to test multiple relative clause types, including subject and object relative clauses [N2-R4]. This format is especially useful when researchers want to elicit spontaneous-like production in a context-rich setting [N2-R4].

### Fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks
These are structured, multiple-choice, or open-ended completion tasks where participants complete a partially completed sentence or choose from options [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. The target clause appears in a grammatically incomplete structure, so the participant’s response is constrained by the task format. These tasks are also used in materials modeled on relative clause production tasks, and they are common in comprehension and test formats [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4].

### Naturalistic elicited production
Naturalistic elicited production is used when the goal is to approximate spontaneous speech and capture variability in relative clause use across contexts [N6-R3][N6-R5]. Unlike sentence repetition or picture description, this method is less controlled and more open-ended, but it is valuable for comparing with corpus data and for studying production in more ecologically valid settings [N6-R3][N6-R5].

---

## 2) What kinds of responses are collected and how they are coded

The response type and coding vary by method:

- **Sentence repetition/imitation**: Responses are produced sentences or phrases that are coded for whether the relative clause is present, correct, or not present, and whether it reflects the intended structure [N6-R2].
- **Picture description**: Responses are spoken or written descriptions that are coded for the presence and type of relative clauses, as well as grammatical correctness or appropriateness to the stimulus [N2-R4].
- **Fill-in-the-blank/sentence-completion tasks**: Responses are typically multiple-choice or open-ended completions, and scoring is based on whether the completed relative clause matches the target structure, especially for subject versus object relative clauses [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4].
- **Naturalistic elicited production**: Responses are spontaneous speech samples, and coding is more challenging because the data are less standardized and may include irrelevant or digressive material [N6-R3].

The branch reports also note that spontaneous speech data are contrasted with elicited production data in experimental studies, with naturalistic data having limitations because the mere emergence of relative clauses may not reflect the underlying construct [N6-R3]. This matters for coding because naturalistic data often require more lenient or context-sensitive coding than tightly controlled elicited responses [N6-R3].

---

## 3) Advantages and limitations of each method

### Sentence repetition/imitation
**Useful for:**  
- Controlled measurement of relative clause production  
- Comparing different relative clause types  
- Measuring specific constructs such as the NPAH effect [N6-R2][N6-R3]

**Limitations:**  
- May produce highly artificial or rehearsed responses [N6-R3]  
- Can reduce ecological validity if the task is too narrow or over-trained [N6-R3]  
- Implementation choices such as repetition frequency and feedback can affect data quality [N6-R2]

### Picture description
**Useful for:**  
- Providing concrete context  
- Testing multiple relative clause types  
- Eliciting spontaneous-like output [N2-R4]

**Limitations:**  
- Output quality can vary widely depending on participants’ language proficiency and instructions [N2-R4]  
- Responses may be difficult to code reliably because participants vary in how much descriptive detail they provide [N2-R4]  
- Can be productive in some cases, but not in others [N2-R3]

### Fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks
**Useful for:**  
- Relatively simple and structured response formats  
- Easy scoring, especially when participants choose among options [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]  
- Controlled context for the target clause [N2-R1][N4-R4]

**Limitations:**  
- May encourage guessing, word-order recall, or grammatical guessing rather than genuine production [N2-R1][N4-R4]  
- Ecological validity is generally lower than in more open-ended formats [N2-R1][N4-R4]  
- Implementation choices such as number of options, distractors, and open-endedness affect scoring and authenticity [N2-R1][N2-R2]

### Naturalistic elicited production
**Useful for:**  
- Capturing spontaneous speech and variability in relative clause use [N6-R3][N6-R5]  
- Comparing with corpus data and studying real-world production [N6-R3][N6-R5]

**Limitations:**  
- Difficult to standardize and prone to irrelevant or digressive material [N6-R3]  
- Subject to observer bias if researchers rely on retrospective or partial sampling [N6-R3]  
- Sampling strategy and corpus comparison matter for whether the data are representative and analyzable [N6-R3][N6-R5]

---

## 4) Task design and participant burden

Task complexity strongly influences elicited output quality. The evidence suggests that more complex or open-ended tasks may reduce the likelihood of mechanical responses but can also introduce noise or inconsistency [N2-R3]. In contrast, more structured formats such as fill-in-the-blank tasks are often easier to score and less burdensome [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. The branch report also notes that task complexity can be reduced in operational execution and site burden domains, which supports the idea that burden-sensitive designs can mitigate negative effects [N5-R1]. Participant burden changes across formats: sentence repetition and picture description are likely to be more burdensome than simple multiple-choice tasks because they require participants to generate speech or longer descriptions [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. Adaptive elicitation and dynamic response sampling are useful for reducing cognitive fatigue and improving data accuracy, but they require careful design to avoid introducing new bias [N5-R5].

Task instructions and feedback also matter. Picture-description tasks require clear instructions to guide participants toward the intended structure [N2-R4]. The evidence on preference elicitation and choice tasks suggests that cognitive burden varies with task design and that feedback can reduce burden and improve accuracy [N5-R3]. The broader point is that even small changes in instructions or feedback can have meaningful effects on performance [N5-R3][N5-R5].

---

## 5) Coding, scoring, and analysis challenges

Common coding and scoring procedures depend on the elicitation method. In sentence repetition/imitation, coding is usually whether the relative clause is present, correct, or not present [N6-R2]. In picture description, responses are coded for presence and type of relative clauses, as well as grammatical correctness or appropriateness to the stimulus [N2-R4]. In fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks, scoring is based on whether the completed relative clause matches the target structure [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. The evidence also indicates that corpus-based analysis and experimental elicitation differ in how they are coded and analyzed [N3-F2].

Intercoder reliability is a central concern. Intercoder reliability refers to the degree to which two analysts agree on their decisions, such as which passages were coded in a particular way [N7-R3]. The branch reports also note that high intercoder reliability is required in qualitative content analysis when multiple coders are involved, and that ICR scores can be used as a heuristic tool in explorative studies [N7-R1][N7-R4]. This implies that coding relative clauses is especially sensitive to annotation bias when coders disagree on grammaticality, clause type, or context-appropriateness [N7-R3][N7-R1][N7-R4].

Corpus and experimental data differ in analysis. Corpus-based studies are useful for capturing large-scale usage patterns and investigating input frequency effects, but they are limited by the rarity of relative clauses in running discourse and by difficulty isolating the construct of interest [N3-F2]. Experimental elicitation is useful for controlling variables and measuring specific constructs, but it can lose ecological validity if the task is too artificial [N3-F2]. Naturalistic data have limitations because the mere emergence of relative clauses may not reflect the underlying construct [N6-R3]. This matters for analysis because corpus data often require frequency-based or distributional analysis, while experimental data may be more suited to item analysis, response coding, or comparison of specific types [N3-F2][N6-R3].

---

## 6) Overall synthesis

In summary, the most commonly used methods for eliciting relative clause production data are:

1. **Sentence repetition/imitation** — highly controlled, useful for direct elicitation and comparison, but can be overly artificial.
2. **Picture description** — context-rich and useful for spontaneous-like production, but variable output quality and coding reliability.
3. **Fill-in-the-blank/sentence-completion tasks** — simple and structured, good for easy scoring, but lower ecological validity.
4. **Naturalistic elicited production** — closest to spontaneous speech, valuable for ecological validity, but harder to standardize and code.

The evidence also shows that **methodological tradeoffs** are central. Corpus-based studies are useful for large-scale usage patterns and input frequency effects, but they are limited by rarity and construct isolation [N3-F2]. Experimental studies are useful for controlled measurement, but they may lose ecological validity [N3-F2]. Adaptive elicitation and dynamic response sampling are useful for reducing burden and improving data accuracy, but they require careful design to avoid bias [N5-R5]. Task complexity affects output quality, participant burden, and performance, with more structured formats usually being less burdensome but less ecologically valid than open-ended ones [N2-R3][N5-R1][N5-R5]. Finally, coding, scoring, and intercoder reliability are central challenges, especially when responses are open-ended or when corpus and experimental data are combined [N7-R3][N7-R1][N7-R4][N3-F2].

In short, the best method depends on the research question: if the goal is precise, controlled comparison, use sentence repetition; if the goal is context-rich production, use picture description; if the goal is easy scoring, use fill-in-the-blank tasks; and if the goal is ecological validity, use naturalistic elicited production. Across all methods, implementation choices, task instructions, feedback, and coding reliability strongly shape data quality [N6-R2][N2-R4][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-R5][N7-R3][N3-F2].

Mini-report on the main elicitation methods used in relative clause studies

The literature most commonly uses a small set of elicitation formats, with sentence repetition/imitation, picture description, and fill-in-the-blank/sentence-completion tasks being especially prominent. A review of relative clause production methods notes that a more controlled production task type is elicited imitation (or sentence repetition), in which participants are asked to repeat what they hear or read [N6-R2]. Picture description is also widely used because it provides concrete context and can be adapted to test multiple relative clause types, such as subject and object clauses, with picture stimuli that depict reversible events [N2-R4]. Fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion formats are likewise common, as they are used in tests and comprehension tasks with blanks and multiple-choice options, and in materials modeled on relative clause production tasks [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. The same search results also point to elicited production as a core method in comparative studies of naturalistic corpora and elicited production experiments [N6-R5].

How each method structures the target clause and surrounding context varies accordingly. In sentence repetition/imitation, the target clause is embedded in a sentence or phrase that participants are asked to repeat, so the context is controlled and highly structured [N6-R2]. In picture description, the context is provided by visual stimuli, and the target clause is often inferred from the pictures rather than being directly stated [N2-R4]. In fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks, the context is usually a partially completed sentence, so the target clause is embedded in a grammatically incomplete structure that participants complete [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. The evidence also suggests that some studies use sentence-repetition tasks to measure the construct underlying an effect such as the NPAH effect, and that these tasks can be adapted to different relative clause types [N6-R2][N6-R4].

What kinds of responses are collected and how they are coded also differ by method. In sentence repetition/imitation, the response is a produced sentence or phrase, and coding typically involves checking whether the produced relative clause is present, correct, or not present, and whether it reflects the intended structure [N6-R2]. In picture-description tasks, responses are spoken or written descriptions that must be coded for the presence and type of relative clauses, and the coding may also assess whether the description is grammatically correct or appropriate given the picture [N2-R4]. In fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks, responses are usually multiple-choice or open-ended completions, and coding is based on whether the completed relative clause matches the target structure, especially for subject versus object relative clauses [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. The evidence also mentions spontaneous speech data, which are collected in naturalistic settings and are contrasted with elicited production data in experimental studies [N6-R3]. That contrast is relevant to coding because naturalistic data may require more lenient or context-sensitive coding than tightly controlled elicited responses [N6-R3].

Overall, the main elicitation formats are sentence repetition/imitation, picture description, fill-in-the-blank/sentence-completion tasks, and naturalistic elicited production. These formats structure the target clause within a controlled or contextualized prompt, and they collect responses that are then coded for relative clause presence, type, and correctness [N6-R2][N2-R4][N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-R4][N6-R3].

Mini-report on task design and participant burden

Task complexity can strongly influence elicited output quality. The evidence suggests that more complex or open-ended tasks may reduce the likelihood of mechanical responses, but also increase the risk of noise or inconsistent output. For example, picture-description tasks are described as being productive in some cases, but they also depend on participants’ ability to generate appropriate descriptions rather than simply selecting a pre-specified answer [N2-R3]. The same source notes that relative clause response types were examined in a table of responses, implying that output quality can vary depending on how clearly participants can produce the target structure [N2-R3]. The task-complexity literature also indicates that complexity can be reduced in operational execution and site burden domains, which is relevant to the idea that more complex elicitation formats may impose greater demands on participants [N5-R1]. This is consistent with the broader claim that task design features and participant characteristics affect study outcomes, including participant burden and data quality [N5-R4].

Participant burden changes across elicitation formats in predictable ways. Elicited production tasks, especially sentence repetition and picture description, are likely to be more burdensome than simple multiple-choice tasks because they require participants to generate speech or longer descriptions. By contrast, fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion formats are often less burdensome because they are shorter and more structured [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N6-R2]. The search results also point to adaptive elicitation and dynamic participant-responsive designs as ways to reduce cognitive fatigue and improve data accuracy, suggesting that burden-sensitive formats can mitigate the negative effects of task complexity [N5-R5]. This is especially important in relative clause studies, where participants may have to generate multiple responses or describe a scene, both of which can increase mental effort [N2-R4][N6-R2].

Task instructions and feedback also affect performance. In the provided evidence, picture-description tasks are used with stimuli that depict reversible events and are associated with multiple relative clause types, indicating that clear instructions are needed to guide participants toward the intended structure [N2-R4]. The literature on preference elicitation and choice tasks also emphasizes that cognitive burden varies with task design, and that feedback can reduce burden and improve accuracy [N5-R3]. While the evidence here is not directly about relative clause studies, it supports the general principle that explicit instructions and responsive feedback can reduce confusion and improve response quality [N5-R3][N5-R5]. The same point is reinforced by the emphasis on participant burden as a hidden constraint in clinical trials, which implies that even small changes in instructions or feedback can have meaningful effects on data collection [N5-R2].

In summary, task complexity can improve output quality when it encourages productive generation, but it can also introduce noise or inconsistency if participants struggle with the task. Participant burden is generally lower in simple, structured formats like fill-in-the-blank tasks and higher in open-ended formats like picture description or sentence repetition. Instructions and feedback matter because they can reduce burden and improve performance, especially when tasks are complex or adaptive [N2-R3][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5].

Mini-report on advantages and limitations of each method

Each method has a distinct usefulness and set of limitations. Sentence repetition/imitation is useful because it is highly controlled and directly measures the target construct, making it suitable for comparing different relative clause types or effects like the NPAH effect [N6-R2][N6-R3]. It is also convenient for collecting speech samples that can be coded for relative clause presence and structure [N6-R2]. Its main limitation is that it may produce highly artificial or rehearsed responses, especially if participants are over-trained or if the task is too narrow [N6-R3]. This can reduce ecological validity and make the data less representative of natural speech [N6-R3]. Implementation choices such as sentence length, repetition frequency, and whether feedback is provided can affect data quality, with more frequent repetition potentially improving accuracy at the cost of burden [N6-R2].

Picture-description tasks are useful because they provide concrete context and can be adapted to test multiple relative clause types, including subject and object clauses, with stimuli that depict reversible events [N2-R4]. They are also good for eliciting spontaneous-like output, as participants are asked to describe a scene rather than simply select an answer [N2-R4]. The limitation is that participants may vary widely in how much descriptive detail they provide, which can make coding less reliable and more context-dependent [N2-R4]. The same evidence also shows that these tasks can be productive in some cases, but not in others, suggesting that output quality is sensitive to participants’ language proficiency and task instructions [N2-R3]. Implementation choices such as stimulus selection, response length, and whether participants are asked to repeat or describe matter for data quality [N2-R4].

Fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks are useful because they are relatively simple, structured, and easy to score, especially when participants choose among options or complete a sentence [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. They are especially suitable for testing relative clause type differences and for controlling the context in which the target clause appears [N2-R1][N4-R4]. However, they are limited in ecological validity because they may encourage guessing, word-order recall, or grammatical guessing rather than genuine production [N2-R1][N4-R4]. Implementation choices such as the number of options, the presence of distractors, and the degree of open-endedness can affect both ease of scoring and the authenticity of the responses [N2-R1][N2-R2].

Naturalistic elicited production is useful when the goal is to approximate spontaneous speech and capture variability in relative clause use across contexts [N6-R3][N6-R5]. It is also valuable for comparing with corpus data and for studying how learners produce relative clauses in real-world settings [N6-R3][N6-R5]. Its main limitation is that spontaneous speech is difficult to standardize and may include irrelevant or digressive material that complicates coding [N6-R3]. It can also be subject to observer bias if researchers rely on retrospective or partial sampling rather than systematic collection [N6-R3]. Implementation choices such as sampling strategy, recording protocol, and corpus comparison can affect whether the data are representative and analyzable [N6-R3][N6-R5].

The evidence also points to broader methodological tradeoffs. Corpus-based studies are useful for capturing large-scale usage patterns and for investigating input frequency effects, but they are limited by the rarity of relative clauses in running discourse and by the difficulty of isolating the construct of interest [N3-F2]. Experimental studies are useful for controlling variables and measuring specific constructs, but they can lose ecological validity if the task is too artificial [N3-F2]. Adaptive elicitation and dynamic response sampling are useful for reducing cognitive fatigue and improving data accuracy, but they require careful design to avoid introducing new sources of bias [N5-R5]. Overall, the most useful methods depend on the research question: controlled imitation is best for direct elicitation and comparison, picture description is best for context-rich production, and naturalistic elicited production is best for ecological validity [N6-R2][N2-R4][N6-R3][N6-R5].

Mini-report on coding, scoring, and analysis challenges

Common coding and scoring procedures for relative clauses depend on the elicitation method. In sentence repetition/imitation, coding typically involves checking whether the produced relative clause is present, correct, or not present, and whether it reflects the intended structure [N6-R2]. In picture-description tasks, responses are coded for the presence and type of relative clauses, as well as for grammatical correctness or appropriateness to the stimulus [N2-R4]. In fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks, scoring is often based on whether the completed relative clause matches the target structure, especially for subject versus object relative clauses [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. The evidence also mentions corpus-based analysis and experimental elicitation, which suggests that coding can be more complex when combining naturalistic and experimental data [N3-F2].

Sources of intercoder reliability and annotation bias are well established in the evidence. Intercoder reliability is defined as the degree to which two analysts or coders agree on their decisions, such as which passages were coded in a particular way [N7-R3]. A separate source states that high intercoder reliability is required in qualitative content analysis when more than one coder is involved, and that ICR scores can be used as a heuristic tool in explorative studies to objectify or specify coding decisions [N7-R1][N7-R4]. This implies that coding relative clauses is especially sensitive to bias if coders differ in how they interpret context, grammatical correctness, or relative clause type. The evidence also suggests that coding and scoring are more challenging when responses are open-ended or when the target structure is ambiguous, because those cases require more judgment [N6-R2][N2-R4].

How corpus and experimental data differ in analysis is a key distinction. ## Integrated final answer on methods for eliciting relative clause production data

The literature on relative clause production data relies on a small set of commonly used elicitation methods, each of which structures the target clause differently and produces different kinds of responses that are then coded in distinct ways. The main formats identified in the branch reports are **sentence repetition/imitation**, **picture description**, **fill-in-the-blank/sentence-completion tasks**, and **naturalistic elicited production** [N6-R2][N2-R4][N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-R5]. These methods are chosen for different research purposes, and each has its own advantages and limitations that affect data quality, ecological validity, and analysis.

---

## 1) Main elicitation methods and how they structure the target clause

### Sentence repetition/imitation
This is one of the most commonly used controlled methods in relative clause studies. Participants are asked to repeat what they hear or read, making it a direct and highly structured way to elicit production [N6-R2]. The target clause is embedded in a sentence or phrase that participants must reproduce, so the context is tightly controlled [N6-R2]. This method is especially useful for comparing different relative clause types or for measuring the construct underlying an effect such as the NPAH effect [N6-R3].

### Picture description
In picture-description tasks, the context is provided by visual stimuli, and participants describe the scene or event depicted in the picture [N2-R4]. The target clause is often inferred from the picture, rather than being directly stated. Because the stimuli can depict reversible events, these tasks can be adapted to test multiple relative clause types, including subject and object relative clauses [N2-R4]. This format is especially useful when researchers want to elicit spontaneous-like production in a context-rich setting [N2-R4].

### Fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks
These are structured, multiple-choice, or open-ended completion tasks where participants complete a partially completed sentence or choose from options [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. The target clause appears in a grammatically incomplete structure, so the participant’s response is constrained by the task format. These tasks are also used in materials modeled on relative clause production tasks, and they are common in comprehension and test formats [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4].

### Naturalistic elicited production
Naturalistic elicited production is used when the goal is to approximate spontaneous speech and capture variability in relative clause use across contexts [N6-R3][N6-R5]. Unlike sentence repetition or picture description, this method is less controlled and more open-ended, but it is valuable for comparing with corpus data and for studying production in more ecologically valid settings [N6-R3][N6-R5].

---

## 2) What kinds of responses are collected and how they are coded

The response type and coding vary by method:

- **Sentence repetition/imitation**: Responses are produced sentences or phrases that are coded for whether the relative clause is present, correct, or not present, and whether it reflects the intended structure [N6-R2].
- **Picture description**: Responses are spoken or written descriptions that are coded for the presence and type of relative clauses, as well as grammatical correctness or appropriateness to the stimulus [N2-R4].
- **Fill-in-the-blank/sentence-completion tasks**: Responses are typically multiple-choice or open-ended completions, and scoring is based on whether the completed relative clause matches the target structure, especially for subject versus object relative clauses [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4].
- **Naturalistic elicited production**: Responses are spontaneous speech samples, and coding is more challenging because the data are less standardized and may include irrelevant or digressive material [N6-R3].

The branch reports also note that spontaneous speech data are contrasted with elicited production data in experimental studies, with naturalistic data having limitations because the mere emergence of relative clauses may not reflect the underlying construct [N6-R3]. This matters for coding because naturalistic data often require more lenient or context-sensitive coding than tightly controlled elicited responses [N6-R3].

---

## 3) Advantages and limitations of each method

### Sentence repetition/imitation
**Useful for:**  
- Controlled measurement of relative clause production  
- Comparing different relative clause types  
- Measuring specific constructs such as the NPAH effect [N6-R2][N6-R3]

**Limitations:**  
- May produce highly artificial or rehearsed responses [N6-R3]  
- Can reduce ecological validity if the task is too narrow or over-trained [N6-R3]  
- Implementation choices such as repetition frequency and feedback can affect data quality [N6-R2]

### Picture description
**Useful for:**  
- Providing concrete context  
- Testing multiple relative clause types  
- Eliciting spontaneous-like output [N2-R4]

**Limitations:**  
- Output quality can vary widely depending on participants’ language proficiency and instructions [N2-R4]  
- Responses may be difficult to code reliably because participants vary in how much descriptive detail they provide [N2-R4]  
- Can be productive in some cases, but not in others [N2-R3]

### Fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks
**Useful for:**  
- Relatively simple and structured response formats  
- Easy scoring, especially when participants choose among options [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]  
- Controlled context for the target clause [N2-R1][N4-R4]

**Limitations:**  
- May encourage guessing, word-order recall, or grammatical guessing rather than genuine production [N2-R1][N4-R4]  
- Ecological validity is generally lower than in more open-ended formats [N2-R1][N4-R4]  
- Implementation choices such as number of options, distractors, and open-endedness affect scoring and authenticity [N2-R1][N2-R2]

### Naturalistic elicited production
**Useful for:**  
- Capturing spontaneous speech and variability in relative clause use [N6-R3][N6-R5]  
- Comparing with corpus data and studying real-world production [N6-R3][N6-R5]

**Limitations:**  
- Difficult to standardize and prone to irrelevant or digressive material [N6-R3]  
- Subject to observer bias if researchers rely on retrospective or partial sampling [N6-R3]

---

## 4) Task design and participant burden

Task complexity strongly influences elicited output quality. The evidence suggests that more complex or open-ended tasks may reduce the likelihood of mechanical responses but can also introduce noise or inconsistency [N2-R3]. In contrast, more structured formats such as fill-in-the-blank tasks are often easier to score and less burdensome [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. The branch report also notes that task complexity can be reduced in operational execution and site burden domains, which supports the idea that burden-sensitive designs can mitigate negative effects [N5-R1]. Adaptive elicitation and dynamic response sampling are useful for reducing cognitive fatigue and improving data accuracy, but they require careful design to avoid introducing new bias [N5-R5].

Task instructions and feedback also matter. Picture-description tasks require clear instructions to guide participants toward the intended structure [N2-R4]. The evidence on preference elicitation and choice tasks suggests that cognitive burden varies with task design and that feedback can reduce burden and improve accuracy [N5-R3]. ---

## 5) Coding, scoring, and analysis challenges

Common coding and scoring procedures depend on the elicitation method. In sentence repetition/imitation, coding is usually whether the relative clause is present, correct, or not present [N6-R2]. In picture description, responses are coded for presence and type of relative clauses, as well as grammatical correctness or appropriateness to the stimulus [N2-R4]. In fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks, scoring is based on whether the completed relative clause matches the target structure [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. The evidence also indicates that corpus-based analysis and experimental elicitation differ in how they are coded and analyzed [N3-F2].

Intercoder reliability is a central concern. Intercoder reliability refers to the degree to which two analysts agree on their decisions, such as which passages were coded in a particular way [N7-R3]. The branch reports also note that high intercoder reliability is required in qualitative content analysis when multiple coders are involved, and that ICR scores can be used as a heuristic tool in explorative studies [N7-R1][N7-R4]. This implies that coding relative clauses is especially sensitive to annotation bias when coders disagree on grammaticality, clause type, or context-appropriateness [N7-R3][N7-R1][N7-R4].

Corpus and experimental data differ in analysis. Corpus-based studies are useful for capturing large-scale usage patterns and investigating input frequency effects, but they are limited by the rarity of relative clauses in running discourse and by difficulty isolating the construct of interest [N3-F2]. Experimental elicitation is useful for controlling variables and measuring specific constructs, but it can lose ecological validity if the task is too artificial [N3-F2]. Naturalistic data have limitations because the mere emergence of relative clauses may not reflect the underlying construct [N6-R3]. This matters for analysis because corpus data often require frequency-based or distributional analysis, while experimental data may be more suited to item analysis, response coding, or comparison of specific types [N3-F2][N6-R3].

---

## 6) Overall synthesis

In summary, the most commonly used methods for eliciting relative clause production data are:

1. **Sentence repetition/imitation** — highly controlled, useful for direct elicitation and comparison, but can be overly artificial.
2. **Picture description** — context-rich and useful for spontaneous-like production, but variable output quality and coding reliability.
3. **Fill-in-the-blank/sentence-completion tasks** — simple and structured, good for easy scoring, but lower ecological validity.
4. **Naturalistic elicited production** — closest to spontaneous speech, valuable for ecological validity, but harder to standardize and code.

The evidence also shows that **methodological tradeoffs** are central. Corpus-based studies are useful for large-scale usage patterns and input frequency effects, but they are limited by rarity and construct isolation [N3-F2]. Experimental studies are useful for controlled measurement, but they may lose ecological validity [N3-F2]. Adaptive elicitation and dynamic response sampling are useful for reducing burden and improving data accuracy, but they require careful design to avoid bias [N5-R5]. Task complexity affects output quality, participant burden, and performance, with more structured formats usually being less burdensome but less ecologically valid than open-ended ones [N2-R3][N5-R1][N5-R5]. Finally, coding, scoring, and intercoder reliability are central challenges, especially when responses are open-ended or when corpus and experimental data are combined [N7-R3][N7-R1][N7-R4][N3-F2].

In short, the best method depends on the research question: if the goal is precise, controlled comparison, use sentence repetition; if the goal is context-rich production, use picture description; if the goal is easy scoring, use fill-in-the-blank tasks; and if the goal is ecological validity, use naturalistic elicited production. In picture-description tasks, responses are spoken or written descriptions that must be coded for the presence and type of relative clauses, and the coding may also assess whether the description is grammatically correct or appropriate given the picture [N2-R4]. Overall, the main elicitation formats are sentence repetition/imitation, picture description, fill-in-the-blank/sentence-completion tasks, and naturalistic elicited production. Mini-report on advantages and limitations of each method

Each method has a distinct usefulness and set of limitations. Sentence repetition/imitation is useful because it is highly controlled and directly measures the target construct, making it suitable for comparing different relative clause types or effects like the NPAH effect [N6-R2][N6-R3]. It is also convenient for collecting speech samples that can be coded for relative clause presence and structure [N6-R2]. Its main limitation is that it may produce highly artificial or rehearsed responses, especially if participants are over-trained or if the task is too narrow [N6-R3]. This can reduce ecological validity and make the data less representative of natural speech [N6-R3]. Implementation choices such as sentence length, repetition frequency, and whether feedback is provided can affect data quality, with more frequent repetition potentially improving accuracy at the cost of burden [N6-R2].

Picture-description tasks are useful because they provide concrete context and can be adapted to test multiple relative clause types, including subject and object clauses, with stimuli that depict reversible events [N2-R4]. They are also good for eliciting spontaneous-like output, as participants are asked to describe a scene rather than simply select an answer [N2-R4]. The limitation is that participants may vary widely in how much descriptive detail they provide, which can make coding less reliable and more context-dependent [N2-R4]. The same evidence also shows that these tasks can be productive in some cases, but not in others, suggesting that output quality is sensitive to participants’ language proficiency and task instructions [N2-R3]. Implementation choices such as stimulus selection, response length, and whether participants are asked to repeat or describe matter for data quality [N2-R4].

Fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks are useful because they are relatively simple, structured, and easy to score, especially when participants choose among options or complete a sentence [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. They are especially suitable for testing relative clause type differences and for controlling the context in which the target clause appears [N2-R1][N4-R4]. However, they are limited in ecological validity because they may encourage guessing, word-order recall, or grammatical guessing rather than genuine production [N2-R1][N4-R4]. Implementation choices such as the number of options, the presence of distractors, and the degree of open-endedness can affect both ease of scoring and the authenticity of the responses [N2-R1][N2-R2].

Naturalistic elicited production is useful when the goal is to approximate spontaneous speech and capture variability in relative clause use across contexts [N6-R3][N6-R5]. It is also valuable for comparing with corpus data and for studying how learners produce relative clauses in real-world settings [N6-R3][N6-R5]. Its main limitation is that spontaneous speech is difficult to standardize and may include irrelevant or digressive material that complicates coding [N6-R3]. It can also be subject to observer bias if researchers rely on retrospective or partial sampling rather than systematic collection [N6-R3]. Implementation choices such as sampling strategy, recording protocol, and corpus comparison can affect whether the data are representative and analyzable [N6-R3][N6-R5].

The evidence also points to broader methodological tradeoffs. Corpus-based studies are useful for capturing large-scale usage patterns and for investigating input frequency effects, but they are limited by the rarity of relative clauses in running discourse and by the difficulty of isolating the construct of interest [N3-F2]. Experimental studies are useful for controlling variables and measuring specific constructs, but they can lose ecological validity if the task is too artificial [N3-F2]. Adaptive elicitation and dynamic response sampling are useful for reducing cognitive fatigue and improving data accuracy, but they require careful design to avoid introducing new sources of bias [N5-R5]. Overall, the most useful methods depend on the research question: controlled imitation is best for direct elicitation and comparison, picture description is best for context-rich production, and naturalistic elicited production is best for ecological validity [N6-R2][N2-R4][N6-R3][N6-R5].

## Integrated final answer on methods for eliciting relative clause production data

The literature on relative clause production data relies on a small set of commonly used elicitation methods, each of which structures the target clause differently and produces different kinds of responses that are then coded in distinct ways. The main formats identified in the branch reports are **sentence repetition/imitation**, **picture description**, **fill-in-the-blank/sentence-completion tasks**, and **naturalistic elicited production** [N6-R2][N2-R4][N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-R5]. These methods are chosen for different research purposes, and each has its own advantages and limitations that affect data quality, ecological validity, and analysis.

---

## 1) Main elicitation methods and how they structure the target clause

### Sentence repetition/imitation
This is one of the most commonly used controlled methods in relative clause studies. Participants are asked to repeat what they hear or read, making it a direct and highly structured way to elicit production [N6-R2]. The target clause is embedded in a sentence or phrase that participants must reproduce, so the context is tightly controlled [N6-R2]. This method is especially useful for comparing different relative clause types or for measuring the construct underlying an effect such as the NPAH effect [N6-R3].

### Picture description
In picture-description tasks, the context is provided by visual stimuli, and participants describe the scene or event depicted in the picture [N2-R4]. The target clause is often inferred from the picture, rather than being directly stated. Because the stimuli can depict reversible events, these tasks can be adapted to test multiple relative clause types, including subject and object relative clauses [N2-R4]. This format is especially useful when researchers want to elicit spontaneous-like production in a context-rich setting [N2-R4].

### Fill-in-the-blank and sentence-completion tasks
These are structured, multiple-choice, or open-ended completion tasks where participants complete a partially completed sentence or choose from options [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4]. The target clause appears in a grammatically incomplete structure, so the participant’s response is constrained by the task format. These tasks are also used in materials modeled on relative clause production tasks, and they are common in comprehension and test formats [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R4].

### Naturalistic elicited production
Naturalistic elicited production is used when the goal is to approximate spontaneous speech and capture variability in relative clause use across contexts [N6-R3][N6-R5]. Unlike sentence repetition or picture description, this method is less controlled and more open-ended, but it is valuable for comparing with corpus data and for studying production in more ecologically valid settings [N6-R3][N6-R5].

---
